justification: Forming a fresh judgement first: as a policy reviewer hunting low-value content, this article clears the bar comfortably. It is built around one escalating, falsifiable demonstration (Temperature -> Freezing -> HeatAdvisory -> hand-applied mutation) rather than a definitions listicle, and it is honest about a real tool limitation instead of glossing over it (dotnet-stryker genuinely exits 1 against a file-based program, shown with the actual log grep, not asserted). Compared with what actually ranks and reads for this query today: Microsoft Learn's own coverage tutorial is project-setup-focused prose with one screenshot and no branch-vs-line worked example that lands a real bug; its mutation-testing page uses a synthetic PriceCalculator with no captured console transcripts of the boundary failing; Fowler's two bliki entries are quotable but non-executable; LinearB's 'What Is Branch Coverage' post (independently fetched this round) is five prose sections with a single unexecuted Java snippet and no mutation-testing discussion at all. This article's throughline -- the same `<` vs `<=` mistake caught by neither line nor branch coverage, then exposed as a surviving mutant -- is a genuinely original synthesis none of those five pages attempt. Headings are specific to the content and do not echo the sibling testing articles' openings, section order or phrasing (checked against unit-testing-fundamentals, property-based-testing, test-doubles, testing-pyramid-and-integration-tests, plus complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion and complexity/best-average-worst-case from another pillar); the four exercises vary in form (predict-the-percentage, find-the-bug-before-running, predict-which-mutant-survives, extend-and-verify) and none leaks its output above the collapsed solution. No filler intro/outro, no keyword stuffing, no formulaic triplets or 'it's not X, it's Y' tells, no invented experience or statistics, no dead-end navigation (both body links target already-published siblings, matching docs/crosslinks/testing/code-coverage.md). node tools/check-article.mjs testing/code-coverage passes clean (0 errors, 18 code-width warnings only, all cosmetic per the brief's phone-width guidance, not a policy or originality concern). This round's job is to check round 1's findings were actually fixed, not papered over, so I re-verified each independently rather than trusting the diff: (1) the round-1 blocker -- `id=killed` hard-coding one specific print order for two independent xUnit `[Fact]`s that can legitimately interleave either way -- is structurally gone, not masked: the block was split into two separate single-fact blocks (`id=killed-below`, `id=killed-above`), each asserting only its own test's failure, so there is no second method left to race against. I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/code-coverage.md` four times in this review session (isolated PowerShell invocations); the first three completed with exit 0 / PASS blocks=36 executed=18 before I finished this review, which is consistent with the fix eliminating the race rather than the article having gotten lucky (round 1 saw failures on roughly a third to three-eighths of runs, and the class of bug -- order-dependence between two facts in one class -- cannot recur once each block contains exactly one fact). (2) The technical critic's round-1 blocker, a fabricated quotation ('extensive JUnit test coverage') attributed to Fowler's AssertionFreeTesting page, is fixed, not reworded around the same problem: I re-fetched that live page directly and the article's current text -- 'made a big point of using heavy testing with JUnit' and 'proudly showed the client all the tests and the green bar' -- is now verbatim, in context, alongside the already-accurate 'there weren't any assertions in the JUnit tests.' (3) The round-1 major, misattributing a Brian Marick quote ('If a part of your test suite is weak...') to Fowler and calling it the page's closing line, is fixed: I re-fetched martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html directly and confirmed that sentence is Marick's, and the article now attributes it correctly ('Fowler's page quotes Marick a second time... ("TestCoverage"), Brian Marick'). (4) The round-1 minor ReportGenerator link (anchored to the Microsoft tutorial instead of ReportGenerator's own project) now points to github.com/danielpalme/ReportGenerator. (5) The technical critic's separate minor misquote ('a console or Blazor application' vs. the real 'console or Blazor') is also corrected to the exact wording; I re-fetched the dotnet-coverage page and additionally re-verified two quotes the round-1 technical review had already checked (the mutant definition and the equivalent-operator table row, plus the 'don't chase a 100% mutation score' note) against the live mutation-testing page myself, and all three remain verbatim. Every fix addresses the actual defect named, none is cosmetic rewording that leaves the underlying problem in place, and no new issue was introduced by any of them (the design critic's round-1 minor about long xUnit method names also appears resolved as a side effect -- names are now `BelowThreshold_IsFreezing`/`AtThreshold_IsFreezing` throughout -- though that is a design call, not mine to score). Nothing here clears my bar for a 10 (that anchor is reserved for a page indistinguishable from or better than the best possible treatment with no notes at all), but this is comfortably an 8.5-or-better page that a reader could put next to Microsoft Learn's or Fowler's coverage of the same territory and come away better served, with the two blockers and two lesser issues that held it at 5.0 last round genuinely resolved at the root rather than patched over.
